title: The Liars' Weekend
teaser: Every year the Ravenmoor family plays a game: two of them must lie all weekend. This year someone burned Grandmother's new will.

booklet.briefing:
Every summer the Ravenmoor family gathers for the Liars' Weekend. On Friday night each of the five grandchildren draws a sealed card. A Truth card means you must tell the truth all weekend. A Lie card means every single thing you say must be false. It's a family tradition, and they take it very seriously.

On Saturday evening, Grandmother Ravenmoor's new will, the one that left everything to the village hospital, was found burned to ash in the library fireplace. The old will, which splits everything between the five grandchildren, is now the only one left.

The game is still on. When the inspector asked each grandchild two questions, each answered according to their card. Only the butler, who dealt the cards, knows how many Lie cards there were. He won't say who drew them.
rules: Each grandchild drew either a Truth card (both of their statements are true) or a Lie card (both of their statements are false).
The butler dealt exactly two Lie cards.
The will was burned in the library by one of the five grandchildren, so the burner went into the library that evening.

suspects.name: Ambrose Ravenmoor
suspects.description: A struggling barrister with expensive tastes.
suspects.motive: Under the old will he gets a fifth of a fortune.
suspects.statement: 1) Clement drew a Lie card. 2) Dulcie never went into the library.

suspects.name: Beatrice Ravenmoor
suspects.description: A doctor at the very village hospital the new will would have funded.
suspects.motive: Hardly any. She'd have been happy with the new will.
suspects.statement: 1) Whoever burned the will drew a Lie card. 2) I never went into the library.

suspects.name: Clement Ravenmoor
suspects.description: Quiet, bookish, always in the library on any other night.
suspects.statement: 1) Beatrice drew a Truth card. 2) I saw Dulcie walk into the library at half past nine.

suspects.name: Dulcie Ravenmoor
suspects.description: Charming, funny and deeply in debt from a failed fashion label.
suspects.motive: The old will would clear her debts in one go.
suspects.statement: 1) Edgar and I drew the same kind of card. 2) I never went into the library.

suspects.name: Edgar Ravenmoor
suspects.description: A cheerful farmer who finds the whole game ridiculous.
suspects.motive: Could use money for a new barn.
suspects.statement: 1) Dulcie and I drew different kinds of card. 2) Ambrose never went near the library.

evidence.title: The butler
evidence.source: Mr. Greaves, who dealt the cards
evidence.body:
“I shuffled five cards on Friday: two Lie and three Truth. Each grandchild took one and showed it to nobody but me.”

“I will not tell you who has which. Madam would never forgive me for spoiling the game.”

evidence.title: The library fireplace
evidence.body:
The new will is ash. A corner that didn't burn shows Grandmother's signature and the words “to the Ravenmoor Cottage Hospital”.

The fire was lit with a match. The match box on the mantelpiece is missing one match. The ash was still warm at 10:15 pm.

evidence.title: Gloves in the hall
evidence.body: A pair of pale lilac evening gloves with soot on the right fingertips. The family agrees they are Dulcie's; she wore them at dinner.
lines: A pair of pale lilac evening gloves with soot on the right fingertips. The family agrees they are Dulcie's; she wore them at dinner.

evidence.title: Mr. Foxy's note on liars
evidence.body:
“A liar's statement is the exact opposite of the truth. If a liar says 'X and I drew the same card', then in fact we drew different cards.”

“Try the statements in pairs. Some pairs can only be true or false together. Some can never both be true.”

questions.explanation: If Dulcie were truthful, she and Edgar would have the same card, so Edgar would be truthful too, but then his 'different cards' would be false. Contradiction. So Dulcie is lying, which means they really drew different cards, so Edgar is truthful.

questions.explanation: One more liar among Ambrose, Beatrice and Clement. If Ambrose were truthful, Clement would be a liar, so Clement's 'Beatrice drew Truth' would be false, making Beatrice a liar too: three liars. Too many. So Ambrose is the liar. Then Clement is truthful (Ambrose's claim is false) and so is Beatrice (Clement's claim is true).

solution.explanation: Dulcie Ravenmoor drew a Lie card on Friday and thought it was the perfect cover: anything she said would be ignored as part of the game. At half past nine she slipped into the library in her evening gloves, struck a match and fed Grandmother's new will to the fire. Clement saw her go in. But the game cuts both ways. Once you work out who holds the Lie cards, every statement becomes evidence, and only Dulcie fits.

chain.step: Dulcie 1 and Edgar 1 can't both be true or both be false. Dulcie can't be truthful without contradiction, so Dulcie lies and Edgar tells the truth.
With exactly two Lie cards, the second liar must be Ambrose; if he were truthful there would be three liars. So Beatrice, Clement and Edgar are truthful.
Beatrice (true): the burner holds a Lie card, so it's Ambrose or Dulcie.
Edgar (true): Ambrose never went near the library. So the burner is Dulcie.
Clement (true) saw Dulcie enter the library at 9:30, and her lilac gloves have soot on them.
